rule_summary: We found no minimum age for foster carers in the 1995 foster care regulations or the 2003 standards. Tusla's pages state none.
legal_citation: S.I. No. 260 of 1995, art 5
notes: The private agencies we read (Orchard, Origins, Foster Care Ireland) ask applicants to be over 25. Search results say Fostering First Ireland asks the same.

rule_summary: Each adopter must be at least 21. If a couple adopt and one of them is the child's parent or relative, only one must be 21.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 33(4), as amended by the Adoption (Amendment) Act 2017, s 16

rule_summary: Tusla sets no upper age limit. It weighs age with health, capacity to meet a child's needs and support networks.
notes: Tusla Fostering Information Guide, May 2026. Tusla's Can I foster page also lists people over 40.

rule_summary: The law sets no upper age. Each adopter must be of an age to be expected to care for the child throughout childhood.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 34(b)
notes: The Adoption Authority and Tusla both say age is a significant factor when assessing suitability.

rule_summary: Single people and couples can foster, whether married, cohabiting or same-sex. Tusla says marital status, sexual orientation and religion do not matter.
notes: Some private agencies add their own rules; for example, Orchard asks couples to have been together 3 years.

rule_summary: A married couple, civil partners or a cohabiting couple can adopt together. A single person can adopt, as can a parent, step-parent or relative of the child.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 33(1)(a), as amended by the Adoption (Amendment) Act 2017, s 16
notes: A sole applicant who is not the child's parent or relative must satisfy the Authority that the adoption is desirable and in the child's best interests (s 33(1)(a)(iii)). A married applicant adopting alone needs the spouse's consent (s 33(3)).

rule_summary: A cohabiting couple means two adults who have lived together as cohabitants for at least 3 years.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 3, as amended by the Adoption (Amendment) Act 2017

rule_summary: Tusla works with carers who are in same-sex relationships, Travellers, of African or Eastern European origin, Muslim, disabled, unemployed, renting, single or over 40.
notes: People with a disability can foster if it does not stop them caring for a child.

rule_summary: Applicants must be habitually resident in Ireland to apply to Tusla for an assessment. The Authority makes a domestic adoption order only for habitually resident applicants.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 37(1) and s 33(5)
notes: Tusla's page adds that adopters should ideally have lived in the State for at least one year before the order.

rule_summary: Tusla considers working foster carers. The main thing is time to meet a child's needs; some children need one carer at home full time.
Each adopter must have adequate financial means to support the child.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 34(c)

rule_summary: Tusla's assessment discusses finances so applicants feel stable. The allowance is for the child, not personal income.
Applicants must give a written report from a registered doctor on their health.
notes: The regulations say 'health board'; Tusla has held these functions since 2014 (Child and Family Agency Act 2013).

rule_summary: Tusla says significant health issues that affect safe care may rule out fostering, but approval is still possible in some cases.
Tusla asks people who have had addiction issues to be recovered for at least 5 years before applying.
notes: Tusla Fostering Information Guide, May 2026.

rule_summary: Each adopter must be in good health. Tusla requires a medical examination as part of the assessment.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 34(b)
notes: The law sets the health test; the medical examination is from Tusla's adoption assessment page.

rule_summary: Renters can foster, in private or local authority housing. What matters is a safe space and a stable home.
notes: Tusla's May 2026 booklet says the same.

rule_summary: Tusla says a child's own bedroom is ideal but not always essential. A home check looks at whether the accommodation suits.
notes: Private agencies are stricter: Orchard and Foster Care Ireland ask for a spare bedroom; Origins asks for a room for each child, though same-gender siblings may share up to age 12.

rule_summary: Tusla lists people who smoke among those who can foster.
notes: Origins will not place a child under 5, or a child with a disability or breathing difficulty, where someone smokes or vapes.

rule_summary: Many foster carers have pets; safety comes first. Dogs covered by the Control of Dogs Regulations face conditions a social worker will discuss.
notes: The booklet names the Control of Dogs Regulations 1991 (unverified title and year).

rule_summary: Generally no more than two children are placed in one foster home at a time. Sibling groups are the exception and are not placed with other fostered children.
legal_citation: National Standards for Foster Care 2003, standard 10.6
notes: The foster care committee must approve any exception before the placement. Read from a copy of the 2003 Department of Health and Children standards hosted by Better Care Network; HIQA's own page refused our reader. HIQA's 2026 inspections still use these standards. 'Health board' now means Tusla.

rule_summary: Applicants must authorise a statement from the Garda Síochána (police) on any convictions for them and other relevant members of their household.
legal_citation: S.I. No. 260 of 1995, art 5(2)(a)(iii)
notes: The regulations say 'health board'; Tusla has held these functions since 2014 (Child and Family Agency Act 2013).

rule_summary: Garda clearance is needed for all adults living in the home, or with significant unsupervised access to it, before approval or a first placement.
legal_citation: National Standards for Foster Care 2003, standard 14a.7
notes: Read from a copy of the 2003 Department of Health and Children standards hosted by Better Care Network; HIQA's own page refused our reader. HIQA's 2026 inspections still use these standards. 'Health board' now means Tusla.

rule_summary: Assessing a foster carer, a relative carer or an adoption applicant is relevant work under the vetting law, so a vetting disclosure from the National Vetting Bureau is needed.
legal_citation: National Vetting Bureau (Children and Vulnerable Persons) Act 2012, s 12 and Sch 1 Pt 1 paras 12 to 14

rule_summary: Tusla says sexual offences, including those about indecent images of children, rule out fostering. Other convictions depend on their nature and timing.
notes: Tusla asks people to disclose convictions early; vetting is done early in the application.

rule_summary: The service checks its own records, and those of equivalent bodies in other countries where the applicants have lived.
legal_citation: National Standards for Foster Care 2003, standard 14a.5
notes: Read from a copy of the 2003 Department of Health and Children standards hosted by Better Care Network; HIQA's own page refused our reader. HIQA's 2026 inspections still use these standards. 'Health board' now means Tusla.

rule_summary: Applicants must name two referees who are not related to them.
notes: The regulations say 'health board'; Tusla has held these functions since 2014 (Child and Family Agency Act 2013).

rule_summary: An authorised person assesses the applicants and their home. A written report goes to a foster care committee, which must be satisfied they are suitable.
legal_citation: S.I. No. 260 of 1995, art 5(2)(b) and (c) and art 5(3)
notes: The regulations say 'health board'; Tusla has held these functions since 2014 (Child and Family Agency Act 2013). Applicants must be told the outcome in writing (art 5(6)).

rule_summary: A qualified social worker does the assessment and involves the whole household. Applicants see the report, can add comments and can choose to meet the committee.
legal_citation: National Standards for Foster Care 2003, standards 14a.3, 14a.8, 14a.9 and 14a.10
notes: Read from a copy of the 2003 Department of Health and Children standards hosted by Better Care Network; HIQA's own page refused our reader. HIQA's 2026 inspections still use these standards. 'Health board' now means Tusla.

rule_summary: Foster care committees include people with child welfare expertise and at least one foster carer. They recommend whether to approve; Tusla decides.
legal_citation: National Standards for Foster Care 2003, standards 23.2 to 23.4; S.I. No. 260 of 1995, art 5(4) and (5)
notes: Tusla's May 2026 booklet says applicants are invited to the meeting and can appeal a decision. Read from a copy of the 2003 Department of Health and Children standards hosted by Better Care Network; HIQA's own page refused our reader. HIQA's 2026 inspections still use these standards. 'Health board' now means Tusla.

rule_summary: Tusla, or an accredited body it arranges, gives information and counselling, assesses eligibility and suitability, and writes a report. An adoption committee then advises the Adoption Authority.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 37(3) and (4) and s 39
notes: Tusla's page says the assessment includes interviews, home visits, a medical examination and Garda vetting.

rule_summary: The Adoption Authority decides whether to issue a declaration of eligibility and suitability. Before refusing, it must let the applicants be heard.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 40(2) and (4)

rule_summary: Applicants must receive appropriate advice, guidance and training on foster care before they are approved.
notes: The regulations say 'health board'; Tusla has held these functions since 2014 (Child and Family Agency Act 2013).

rule_summary: Tusla asks every applicant to complete a fostering induction course before approval.
notes: Tusla's pages give no length. Search results show an older Tusla booklet describing a 3-day course (unverified).

rule_summary: Each adopter must have had appropriate information, advice and counselling about adoption.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 34(d)

rule_summary: Intercountry adoption applicants register for a Tusla adoption preparation course during assessment.
notes: Tusla's intercountry page lists the workshop as stage four of eight.

rule_summary: Applicants and carers commit to training. Each carer review looks at training needs, which shape the next year's programme.
legal_citation: National Standards for Foster Care 2003, standards 16.6 and 16.9
notes: Tusla says training is compulsory for all foster carers. Read from a copy of the 2003 Department of Health and Children standards hosted by Better Care Network; HIQA's own page refused our reader. HIQA's 2026 inspections still use these standards. 'Health board' now means Tusla.

rule_summary: Tusla's types of foster care include emergency, short-term (up to six months), respite, pre-adoptive, long-term, day fostering, sibling placements, supported lodgings for ages 16 and over, and care of separated children seeking asylum.
notes: The May 2026 booklet lists the same types.

rule_summary: A foster parent is someone other than a relative who cares for a child on Tusla's behalf. Care by relatives is a separate route under its own regulations.
legal_citation: Child Care Act 1991, s 36(1) and (2) and s 41

rule_summary: There are four kinds of domestic adoption: infant adoption, step-parent adoption, relative adoption and long-term foster care to adoption.
notes: For intercountry adoption, the Authority says the country must operate under the Hague Convention and have a programme with Ireland.

rule_summary: A declaration of eligibility and suitability expires after 24 months. The Authority can extend it by up to 12 months on request.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 41(1)

rule_summary: The first review of a foster carer is one year after the first placement. Later reviews are every three years and update Garda checks.
legal_citation: National Standards for Foster Care 2003, standards 17.1 and 17.2
notes: Read from a copy of the 2003 Department of Health and Children standards hosted by Better Care Network; HIQA's own page refused our reader. HIQA's 2026 inspections still use these standards. 'Health board' now means Tusla.

rule_summary: Reviews look at the carer's care, training, changes in circumstances and health. The outcome goes to the foster care committee.
legal_citation: National Standards for Foster Care 2003, standards 17.3, 17.10 and 23.2
notes: Read from a copy of the 2003 Department of Health and Children standards hosted by Better Care Network; HIQA's own page refused our reader. HIQA's 2026 inspections still use these standards. 'Health board' now means Tusla.

rule_summary: The assessment should be done within 16 weeks of the formal application, unless more time is needed. Applicants are told why and given a new date.
legal_citation: National Standards for Foster Care 2003, standard 14a.4
notes: The same rule applies to relatives (14b.5). Read from a copy of the 2003 Department of Health and Children standards hosted by Better Care Network; HIQA's own page refused our reader. HIQA's 2026 inspections still use these standards. 'Health board' now means Tusla.

rule_summary: Tusla says the adoption assessment takes at least 18 months, depending on circumstances.
Tusla says an intercountry adoption is likely to take at least two years.
Relatives who care for a child for Tusla need the same checks: a doctor's report, two unrelated referees, Garda checks, a home assessment, a committee and training.
notes: A relative includes a relative's spouse and anyone who has acted in loco parentis (art 3). The regulations say 'health board'; Tusla has held these functions since 2014 (Child and Family Agency Act 2013).

rule_summary: In an emergency Tusla can place a child with relatives after an interview, a home visit and other enquiries. The full checks must follow within 12 weeks.
legal_citation: S.I. No. 261 of 1995, art 6
notes: The regulations say 'health board'; Tusla has held these functions since 2014 (Child and Family Agency Act 2013).

rule_summary: A step-parent can apply to adopt once the child has lived with the parent and step-parent for at least 2 years.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 37(5) and (6), inserted by the Adoption (Amendment) Act 2017
notes: The Authority can accept an earlier application in particular circumstances (s 37(6)).

rule_summary: Tusla pays a weekly foster care allowance of EUR 400 for each child aged 0 to 12.
notes: The allowance does not affect tax or state benefits. The start date comes from a gov.ie Budget 2025 speech seen only in search results (unverified). A news report says Budget 2027 extends it to age 19 for those in school (unverified).

rule_summary: Tusla pays a weekly foster care allowance of EUR 425 for each child aged 12 and over.
notes: Tusla's page says '0 to 12 years' and '12 years and over', so the boundary at 12 is unclear. Orchard's page says 'up to EUR 425'.

rule_summary: Tusla must pay foster carers an allowance of at least the amount the Minister sets. It may give other financial help.
legal_citation: S.I. No. 260 of 1995, art 14
notes: The regulations say 'health board'; Tusla has held these functions since 2014 (Child and Family Agency Act 2013).

rule_summary: Adoptive Benefit, a social insurance payment for adopters, has a weekly rate of EUR 299 from 5 January 2026.
legal_citation: Social Welfare and Automatic Enrolment Retirement Savings System (Amendment) Act 2025, s 4
notes: Amends the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005, s 60(1)(b). Search results say it is paid for 24 weeks to people with enough PRSI (social insurance) contributions; not checked on gov.ie, which refused our reader.

rule_summary: Foster care payments from Tusla are exempt from income tax and the Universal Social Charge.
legal_citation: Taxes Consolidation Act 1997, s 192BA
notes: Revenue page published 2 June 2026. The section number comes from search results: s 192BA replaced s 192B in 2019.

rule_summary: Every child in foster care gets their own medical card. Carers can claim child benefit for each child.
notes: Tusla also lists a link worker, a year's IFCA membership and an out-of-hours phone service.

rule_summary: Tusla must provide foster carers with support, including advice, guidance and training.
legal_citation: S.I. No. 260 of 1995, art 15
notes: The 2003 standards add a link worker, local support groups and an out-of-hours service (standards 15, 15.8 and 15.9).

rule_summary: Foster carers must give Tusla at least 28 days' notice before moving home.
notes: The regulations say 'health board'; Tusla has held these functions since 2014 (Child and Family Agency Act 2013).

rule_summary: Tusla advises waiting 12 months after fertility treatment before applying to foster.
notes: Tusla Fostering Information Guide, May 2026.

rule_summary: Tusla tries to place children who are at least two years younger than the carer's youngest child.
notes: Origins asks for the same two-year gap.

rule_summary: Tusla should try to respect a guardian's wishes on the child's religious upbringing and the religion of the foster carers.
legal_citation: S.I. No. 260 of 1995, art 8
notes: For adoption, people giving consent must be told the adopters' religion if they differ (Tusla and Adoption Authority pages).

rule_summary: A foster carer or relative who has cared for a child for at least 5 years can ask a court for enhanced rights, with Tusla's consent.
legal_citation: Child Care Act 1991, s 43A
notes: The Child Care (Amendment) Bill 2025 (Bill 78 of 2025) would cut this to 3 years. It reached Dáil Second Stage in January 2026; the revised Act still said 5 years in November 2026.

rule_summary: Foster carers can seek to adopt a child without parental consent, through the High Court, if the child has lived with them for at least 18 months and the parents have failed the child for at least 36 months.
legal_citation: Adoption Act 2010, s 54(2A), as amended by the Adoption (Amendment) Act 2017
notes: The court must also be satisfied that adoption is a proportionate response.

rule_summary: Tusla may use non-statutory (private or voluntary) agencies only under a service agreement, and must check they meet the regulations and standards.
legal_citation: S.I. No. 260 of 1995, art 24; National Standards for Foster Care 2003, standards 24.2, 24.3 and 24.6
notes: Tusla's Alternative Care Inspection and Monitoring Service approves and monitors these agencies and listed five in November 2026. HIQA also inspects them against the 2003 standards. We found no separate registration law for them.
